title: Async/Await
description: Master asynchronous programming in C# with async/await, Task, and Task<T> for non-blocking, responsive applications.

data.text: Asynchronous programming allows your application to stay responsive while waiting for long-running operations to complete — such as network calls, file I/O, or database queries. Instead of blocking the calling thread, async/await frees it up to do other work and resumes execution when the operation finishes.

In a synchronous model, each line of code waits for the previous one to fully finish before running. If a network call takes three seconds, the entire thread — and in UI apps, the whole interface — is frozen. Asynchronous code releases the thread during the wait and resumes when data is ready, keeping the application fluid and responsive.

data.caption: Comparing synchronous blocking versus asynchronous non-blocking execution
data.definition:
sequenceDiagram
    participant U as User / Caller
    participant T as Thread
    participant N as Network/IO

    Note over U,N: Synchronous (blocking)
    U->>T: Request data
    T->>N: Send request
    N-->>T: [3s wait — thread blocked]
    T-->>U: Return data

    Note over U,N: Asynchronous (non-blocking)
    U->>T: Request data async
    T->>N: Send request
    N-->>T: [thread freed — can serve other work]
    N-->>T: Data ready — resume here
    T-->>U: Return data

data.text: An async method returns Task (for operations with no return value) or Task<TResult> (for operations that return a value). The await keyword pauses execution of that method without blocking the thread — the compiler transforms the rest of the method into a continuation that resumes automatically when the awaited task completes.

data.title: Async Method — Fetching Data from an API
data.content: Demonstrates the async/await pattern with HttpClient

data.text: Task represents an ongoing or completed operation that does not produce a return value. Task<TResult> represents an operation that will eventually produce a value of type TResult. Both have useful properties like IsCompleted, IsCanceled, and IsFaulted, and can be awaited, chained with ContinueWith, or run concurrently with Task.WhenAll.

data.title: Task and Task<TResult> in Practice
data.content: Shows fire-and-forget, value-returning, and concurrent task execution

data.text: An async method can return in three ways: by reaching a return statement (the compiler wraps the value in a completed Task<TResult>), by reaching the end of the method (equivalent to returning default), or by throwing an exception that is captured inside the returned Task. Exceptions thrown inside an async method are not thrown on the calling thread — they are stored in the Task and re-thrown when the caller awaits or accesses the Result property.

data.title: How Exceptions Propagate in async Methods
data.content: Demonstrates exception capture and re-throw on await

data.text: Task.WhenAll accepts a collection of tasks and returns a single task that completes when all of them finish. If any task faults, the returned task faults too (with an AggregateException in .NET Framework, or the first exception in .NET 6+). Task.WhenAny completes as soon as the first of the supplied tasks finishes, returning that task.

data.title: Parallel API Calls with Task.WhenAll
data.content: Fetching data from multiple endpoints concurrently

data.text: By default, await captures the current synchronization context and tries to resume on it. In UI apps (WinForms, WPF) this ensures UI updates happen on the main thread. In ASP.NET (pre-Core) and some test environments, capturing the context can cause deadlocks when code blocks the context with .Result or .Wait(). Use ConfigureAwait(false) in library code to skip context capture and avoid deadlocks.

data.title: Never Block on Async Code
data.text: Avoid .Result and .Wait() on Tasks in application code. They block the thread, can cause deadlocks, and defeat the purpose of async. Always use await all the way up the call stack.

ValueTask<T> is a value-type alternative to Task<TResult> designed for hot paths where the result is often already available synchronously (e.g., from an in-memory cache). It avoids heap allocation in the synchronous path but adds complexity — only use it after profiling shows Task<TResult> allocations are a real bottleneck.

cards.title: Task<TResult>
cards.description: Reference type. Always heap-allocated. The standard and recommended choice.

cards.title: ValueTask<TResult>
cards.description: Value type. Avoids allocation when the result is available immediately.
pros: No allocation on the synchronous path

data.title: Exercise: Concurrent File Reader
data.description: Build an async tool that reads multiple text files concurrently and returns the total line count.
steps: Create a method ReadFileLinesAsync(string path) that returns Task<int>.
Use StreamReader and ReadToEndAsync inside the method — do not use blocking reads.
Create a list of at least 3 file paths to read.
Start all ReadFileLinesAsync calls without awaiting them yet.
Use Task.WhenAll to await all reads simultaneously.
Sum up the line counts and print the total.
Measure elapsed time and compare it to reading files sequentially (one after another).
data.expectedOutcome: A working async file reader that demonstrates how concurrent I/O dramatically reduces total wait time compared to sequential processing.

items.question: Can an async method not use await?
items.answer: Yes — but the compiler will warn you, and the method runs synchronously. The only legitimate exception is an async method that returns a cached or already-completed Task.FromResult(value).

items.question: Does async/await create new threads?
items.answer: No — async/await does not create threads. It uses the existing thread pool and returns threads to the pool while waiting for I/O. The continuation may run on a different thread, but no new thread is created for the wait itself.

items.question: What is the difference between Task.Run and await?
items.answer: Task.Run offloads CPU-bound work to a thread-pool thread — useful for compute-heavy operations. await releases the thread while waiting for I/O (network, disk, database). Mix them: await Task.Run(CpuBoundWork) for CPU-bound async.

items.question: Should every method in my app be async?
items.answer: No — only methods that perform I/O-bound or CPU-bound work benefit from async. Simple getters, property accessors, and pure calculations should remain synchronous. Async adds complexity and should be used intentionally.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: async/await enables non-blocking I/O without thread blocking
async Task for fire-and-forget or void-returning operations
async Task<T> for operations that produce a value
await pauses the method, not the thread — the thread returns to the pool
ConfigureAwait(false) prevents deadlocks in library code
data.takeaway: Async/await is essential for building responsive applications. The pattern is simple, but the mental model — cooperative, non-blocking concurrency — takes practice to internalize.
